                      fig.width = 5, fig.height = 2.6, fig.align = "center")
options(width = 80, tibble.print_max = 5, tibble.print_min = 5, pillar.sigfig = 6)
library(tidyverse)

For each task: the code, its output, and what to look for. The data has 20,640 districts.

Install each package once per computer; load it in every session.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("tidyverse")
```

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/touseefhameed/",
              "oka2015-applied-data-science/main/assignment1/data/housing.csv")
housing <- read_csv(url)
```

## Task 1: types of data

```{r}
glimpse(housing)
```

a. Nine columns are quantitative (`<dbl>`). `ocean_proximity` is categorical (`<chr>`).
b. `housing_median_age` counts whole years, so it is discrete. `ocean_proximity` has no
natural order, so it is nominal.
c. Cross-sectional: many districts at one point in time (the 1990 census).

## Task 2: a frequency table

```{r}
housing |>
  count(ocean_proximity, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))
```

ISLAND has only 5 districts. Any average for that group rests on five values, so it should
be reported with its `n` and read with care.

## Task 3: shape

```{r}
hist(housing$median_income)
hist(housing$housing_median_age)
mean(housing$median_income)
median(housing$median_income)
mean(housing$housing_median_age)
median(housing$housing_median_age)
```

`median_income` is skewed right: mean 3.87 above median 3.54. `housing_median_age` is
roughly symmetric, mean 28.6 close to median 29, with a spike at 52, the highest value in
the data.

## Task 4: centre

```{r}
mean(housing$median_house_value)
median(housing$median_house_value)
housing |> count(median_house_value, sort = TRUE)
```

Mean 206,856 above median 179,700: skewed right. The mode is 500,001, in 965 districts.
This value is a ceiling in the data, see Task 7.

```{r}
housing |>
  group_by(ocean_proximity) |>
  summarise(
    mean   = mean(median_house_value),
    median = median(median_house_value),
    n      = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(median))
```

ISLAND has the highest median, 414,700, but from 5 districts. Of the large groups,
NEAR BAY is highest at 233,800; INLAND is far lowest at 108,500.

## Task 5: spread

```{r}
sd(housing$median_house_value)
range(housing$median_house_value)
IQR(housing$median_house_value)
summary(housing$median_house_value)
```

The maximum, 500,001, appears 965 times: values above it were
recorded as 500,001.

## Task 6: missing values

```{r}
colSums(is.na(housing))
hist(housing$total_bedrooms)
housing_filled <- housing |>
  mutate(total_bedrooms = replace_na(total_bedrooms,
                                     median(total_bedrooms, na.rm = TRUE)))
sum(is.na(housing_filled$total_bedrooms))
```

`total_bedrooms` has 207 missing values. It is strongly skewed right (mean 538, median
435), so the median is the better choice.

## Task 7: outliers

```{r}
boxplot(housing$median_house_value)
quantile(housing$median_house_value, c(0.25, 0.75))
IQR(housing$median_house_value)
housing |>
  filter(median_house_value < -98087.5 |
         median_house_value > 482412.5) |>
  nrow()
housing |> filter(median_house_value == 500001) |> nrow()
```

Fences: 119,600 - 1.5 × 145,125 = -98,087.5 and 264,725 + 1.5 × 145,125 = 482,412.5.
1,071 districts lie above the upper fence, 965 of them at exactly 500,001. Those 965 are
not wrong, but their true value is unknown: somewhere at or above 500,001. Keep them and
say so, or remove them when a task needs exact values, and state which you did.

```{r}
m <- mean(housing$total_rooms)
s <- sd(housing$total_rooms)
housing |>
  mutate(z = (total_rooms - m) / s) |>
  filter(abs(z) > 3) |>
  nrow()
```

373 districts have `total_rooms` more than 3 sd from the mean: large districts, not errors.

## Task 8: association

```{r}
plot(housing$median_income, housing$median_house_value)
cor(housing$median_income, housing$median_house_value)
housing |>
  select(income = median_income, value = median_house_value,
         age = housing_median_age, population) |>
  cor() |>
  round(2)
```

a. An upward cloud, with a flat line of points at 500,001 along the top.
b. $r = 0.69$: a fairly strong positive relationship.
c. The weakest pair is income and population: $r = 0.00$. `select(new = old)` renames the
columns so that the matrix fits on the page.
d. No. Correlation shows that the two move together, not why. Richer people may buy in
expensive areas, expensive areas may attract richer people, or a third factor, such as
distance to the coast, may drive both.
